questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13938412/assets/dc708da9adb4f61161ee1face89403bf1a6ce9762905e8a59b4b3ed9031c817a.png)

Consider the picture above. Given that $r=\lambda p+\mu q$, find $\lambda $ and $\mu .$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13938412/assets/84f8951c4921eca20b00132996dc7b2dfafe047d58574e1822da795e1444c861.png)

In $△OPR$ shown above, we have 

- $OP=3|p|$

- $\overset{\to }{OP}$ has the opposite direction to $p$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{OP}=-3p.$

Similarly:

- $PR=2|q|$

- $\overset{\to }{PR}$ has the opposite direction to $q$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PR}=-2q.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PR} \\  & =-3p-2q.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $r=\lambda p+\mu q=-3p-2q.$

Since $p∦q,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

- $\lambda =-3$ and $\mu =-2$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Scalar Factor When Direction Reverses
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13938412/assets/28faea3a553c505a8a5ab9bc7dd6e784dd23a47c336c70d31218fbe249d57cff.png)

Consider the picture above. Given that $c=\lambda a+3b,$ find $\lambda .$
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a+3b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $3b.$ So, we first draw the vector $3b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13938412/assets/52421034c2919620a0a9aae844db0eba2d396e5d6f1152d69bee40ff56c4d8ad.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $3b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=3|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=-3a.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =3b-3a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a+3b=-3a+3b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =-3
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13938412/assets/84ba52159416b3b420daa1ebd82dccac2411aee420201b9b9604937995d9553c.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OS}=s,$ $\overset{\to }{OT}=t,$ and $L$ divides $\overset{―}{ST}$ in the ratio $SL:LT=11:4.$ Express $\overset{\to }{OL}$ via the vectors $s$ and $t.$

$\,\overset{\to }{OL}=$
{{field-1}}
$s+$
{{field-2}}
$t$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OL}=\overset{\to }{OS}+\overset{\to }{SL}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OS}=s,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{SL}.$

First, from $△OST,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{ST} & =\overset{\to }{SO}+\overset{\to }{OT} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OS}+\overset{\to }{OT} \\  & =-s+t \\  & =t-s.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $SL:LT=11:4,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{SL}=\frac{11}{15}\overset{\to }{ST}=\frac{11}{15}(t-s).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OL} & =\overset{\to }{OS}+\overset{\to }{SL} \\  & =s+\frac{11}{15}(t-s) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}s+\frac{11}{15}t.\end{aligned}
$$
